hook: Most buyers burn 3 of their 7 option days.

scores.worst_problem: The hook gives away its own payoff structurally — 'burn 3 of their 7 days' names both the number and the outcome, so a reader can half-guess the answer (inspector scheduling delays) without swiping.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1 to withhold the number or the cause — e.g. 'Your 7 day option period is really 4' — and tighten the weak loop 'Fewer days than you think' into something that names a concrete unseen cost, like 'Two days are already gone.'

deck.hook: Most buyers burn 3 of their 7 option days.

points.title: The Clock Starts Early
body: Your option period starts the day the contract is executed.
Not the day you book the inspection. Not the day you feel ready.
points.loop: It ends at a strange hour.

points.title: The 5 PM Wall
body: The deadline is 5 PM on the last day, not midnight.
Miss it by ten minutes and your right to walk is gone.

points.title: Where 3 Days Go
body: Good inspectors are booked 2 to 3 days out.
The report usually lands a day after they walk the house.
That is 3 of your 7 days spent before you learn a single thing.

points.title: The Fee Buys One Thing
body: The option fee buys the right to walk for any reason at all.
It does not buy repairs and it does not buy a price cut.
Whether it gets credited back at closing is a checkbox most people never read.

points.title: Nobody Has To Fix It
body: An inspection report does not obligate a seller to repair anything.
You ask, they can say no, and then you decide before the clock runs out.
points.loop: You are not out of moves.

points.title: You Can Buy Time
body: An extension has to be agreed in writing before the current period expires.
It usually costs another fee, and the seller can refuse.
Ask at 4:55 on the last day and the answer is no.

linkedinCaption:
The Texas option period is the most misunderstood clause in the contract. It starts the day the contract is executed, not the day the buyer books an inspection. It ends at 5 PM on the final day, not midnight.

The math is unforgiving. Good inspectors are booked two to three days out, and the report often lands a day after they walk the house. On a seven day option, three days are gone before the buyer learns anything.

The fee buys one thing. The right to terminate for any reason. It does not obligate a seller to repair anything or reduce the price.

For the agents here: what option period length are you writing in this market, and why?
